name: big-ball-of-mud
intent: Records what a Big Ball of Mud costs: a system whose organisation is dictated by expediency rather than design, where information is shared promiscuously among distant parts until it is global or duplicated — and the price is that no structural change is affordable, so the only available move is to patch and keep it working.
problem: The system grew by repeated expedient repair, or it was a throwaway prototype that was never thrown away, and its shearing layers cut across the grain of whatever structure it had. Nobody can name the architecture because it was never defined, or it eroded beyond recognition, so any change is local and every local change is a risk to everything else.
context: Foote and Yoder's definition is the reference one: a haphazardly structured, sprawling, sloppy, duct-tape-and-baling-wire spaghetti-code jungle whose code shows unmistakable signs of unregulated growth and repeated expedient repair, with information shared promiscuously among distant elements of the system often to the point where nearly all the important information becomes global or duplicated. Its overall structure may never have been well defined; if it was, it may have eroded beyond recognition. Their crucial contribution is that they do not present this as a straw man — they argue that good programmers build these, that it is a pervasive recurring solution rather than an aberration, and that its appeal is real: a casual, undifferentiated structure lets you address a force between two parts directly without undermining grander architectural aspirations. They describe seven patterns: Big Ball of Mud, Throwaway Code, Piecemeal Growth, Keep It Working, Shearing Layers, Sweeping It Under The Rug, and Reconstruction.
benefits: It is an honest description rather than an insult: unlike 'bad code', this names a specific lifecycle — throwaway code that was kept, piecemeal growth that never met a consolidation phase — and each of those has a known counter-move.

It explains the forces rather than the symptoms. Because the pattern is presented as a pattern, it tells you that a mud system is the path of least resistance against the forces that are actually applied, which is why exhorting 'design it properly' does not work.

It names the only three real responses: keep the system healthy by alternating exploration with consolidation, let it happen deliberately during the prototype and expansion phases, or plan a reconstruction. Anything else is pretending.
It legitimises the fact that mud systems ship: Foote and Yoder argue that the economics of software may make long-term architectural ambition foolhardy, so the cost is recognised rather than denied.
tradeoffs: Consolidation is the answer and consolidation is expensive. Foote and Yoder are explicit that a permanent commitment to refactoring must be made to counteract the forces, and that this is chronic work competing with the acute, local concerns that keep it working — which is exactly why mud is common.

The low-friction property is real and is lost on consolidation. A change touching two distant parts of a mud system can be made directly; the same change in a structured system may require going through the abstractions that were introduced precisely to make such changes safe.

Reconstruction usually fails and the literature says so. The recommended reconstruction is a strangler-fig-style facade over the quarantined mess, with intention-revealing selectors on top, and the authors are realistic that redesigns are routinely rejected for budget — the same dynamic that produces mud in the first place.
Sweeping it under the rug buys time and accumulates debt: quarantining messy code behind a facade gives it a congenial face, but the mess is still there and will be exposed again.

Early mud is legitimate. Foote and Yoder argue a casual structure is emblematic of the prototype and expansion phases, while programmers and users learn the domain's grain — so the same structure that is a defect in year five is a reasonable stance in month three.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the system while the smell is present. The axes that bottom out are discoverability and coupling: nothing in the structure tells you where a piece of knowledge lives, and the dependency graph is a blob rather than a layering. Simplicity is mid rather than low because the local change is genuinely cheap — the system is not complex to operate, it is complex to change — which is exactly the trade Foote and Yoder describe when they call mud's casual structure a secret advantage.

participants.responsibility: Holds the domain knowledge that is shared promiscuously among distant elements, usually as globals or duplicated copies, so no single place owns it.
participants.notes: Its structure is dictated by expediency; if there was ever an architecture, it has eroded beyond recognition.

participants.responsibility: The schedule, budget or business pressure that makes the expedient local fix cheaper than the structural one.
participants.notes: Foote and Yoder trace mud to throwaway code kept because "it works, so why fix it?", and to piecemeal growth driven by keep-it-working.

participants.responsibility: Content with the inertia of the day-to-day chore of patching the holes in failing dikes, and the person whose continuity keeps the tacit knowledge alive.
participants.notes: Foote and Yoder observe that only those unconcerned with architecture, or comfortable with the inertia, are content to work in these.

use_cases: A prototype from a hackathon or a POC that shipped and now has users, with no architecture and no plan to acquire one.
A mature system whose every feature added another vertical slice through the whole stack, so no layer can be changed without touching all of them.
A codebase where 'where does X live?' has no answer, and the only reliable method is asking someone who has worked there for a decade.
A system with several generations of technology in parallel after successive rewrites, none of which completed.
A codebase whose shared state is global or duplicated across modules, so a change in one place silently invalidates a copy elsewhere.
avoid_when: The system is genuinely in its prototype or expansion phase, when learning the domain's grain matters more than committing to a structure — this is Foote and Yoder's own position that it is okay to look like mud 'until you know better'.
The codebase will be replaced or deleted within a known short horizon, in which case consolidation has no return.
The domain is not yet understood, so any structure chosen now is likely to be wrong; explore first, commit later.
The team is small and the change rate is low, so the coordination cost of a real architecture exceeds its benefit — a module monolith with real boundaries may be enough.

The knowledge that is missing is tacit and uncapturable; a written architecture will be fiction until someone can explain the decisions, and forcing one produces a mud system with extra documentation.
pitfalls: Calling it 'technical debt' and doing nothing. Debt has an interest rate; mud is closer to a structural absence, and no amount of documenting the existing arrangement turns a blob into a structure.
Big-bang rewrite. It is the response most often chosen and the one the literature consistently reports as failing; the documented alternative is reconstruction behind a facade, incrementally.
Consolidating the code without consolidating the knowledge, producing the same blob with more layers and no more clarity.
Choosing the architecture from a diagram rather than from the grain of the domain, which is how a structured system becomes a differently shaped mud.
Confusing 'no architecture' with 'no architecture on purpose'. The deliberate absence of architecture is a decision with a cost; the mud version is an accumulation of decisions nobody made.

related_patterns_notes.module: A module is the smallest unit of structure that can be imposed on a mud system without a rewrite, and it is Foote and Yoder's consolidation mechanism in practice: hem in unregulated growth by giving each area a name and an export surface.
related_patterns_notes.facade: A facade is the first step of the documented reconstruction path: put a congenial face on the unpleasantness that has been swept under the rug, then expose it through intention-revealing selectors.
related_patterns_notes.transaction-script: A transaction script is what a mud system gradually grows into when nobody decides on a domain model: one procedure per business operation, which is coherent until the shared rules begin to be duplicated across procedures.
related_patterns_notes.domain-model: A domain model is what emerges once the system's grain is understood — introducing one before then produces structure that does not match the domain and becomes another layer of mud.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: A plugin or extension point is the tool for hemming in growth in a mud: giving one area a declared interface gives the unregulated growth a place to attach that does not require editing the surrounding code.

anti_patterns: The kept prototype: throwaway code that takes on a life of its own because it works and nobody scheduled its removal.
Piecemeal growth without consolidation: features added continuously and no refactoring phase ever scheduled, so the structure erodes by degrees.
The 'keep it working' strategy applied for years: every local change is made to minimise immediate risk, and the chronic architectural risk accumulates unopposed.
Global or duplicated shared knowledge: the same rule or data expressed in several distant places, so no one can be authoritative about it.
Shearing layers: successive changes cut across the existing grain of the system until the structure is undermined.
Sweeping it under the rug: quarantining messy code behind a facade and never going back, so the debt is deferred rather than paid.
The interrupted rewrite: a redesign that was funded, partially applied and then stopped, leaving the system with two incomplete architectures and neither's benefits.
Big-bang rewrite as the default response to mud, which usually produces the same mud with a new technology.
design_principles: Alternate exploration with consolidation, explicitly: the prototype and expansion phases benefit from a casual structure, and the consolidation phase is what pays for it later — skipping it is what produces mud.

Free freedom from choice early: Foote and Yoder note that constraining the design space, as regular columns constrain a building's spaces, can increase reuse, because fewer alternatives have to be considered.
Structure what changes together: an architecture is a statement about which changes are expected to be local, and mud is the statement that every change is global.
Locality of knowledge: information belongs to one place and is shared by reference or contract, never by global variables or by duplication.
Reconstruction incrementally, behind a facade: put a face on the mess, seal it, and improve it from the edge inward.
best_practices: Adopt the Foote and Yoder trichotomy deliberately: keep the system healthy by alternating expansion and consolidation; let it be mud on purpose during exploration; or plan a reconstruction. Pick one explicitly rather than drifting into mud.
Schedule consolidation as a named phase with its own budget, not as leftovers between features — the absence of that budget is the mechanism, not the excuse.

Take mud's one real advantage and preserve it: any force between two distant parts should be addressable directly. When you impose layers, check that a simple change can still be made without going through five abstractions.
Quarantine and facade before you refactor: sweep the mess under the rug behind a stable face first, so the system stays operable while the interior improves.
Start with the seams, not the layers: identify the few places where knowledge is genuinely global or duplicated, give each an owner, and work outward from there.
Treat documentation as a finding tool, not a deliverable — the first useful artefact is an honest map of where things actually live, which is usually surprising.
Protect the grain: before restructuring, find out which modules change together and use that as the boundary. A structure that contradicts the change pattern is another mud.
Sunlight is the most effective enemy: code review and pair programming expose the tangle while it is still small, which is the mechanism Foote and Yoder name against the pattern.
Set a decision to reconstruct before the cost of the rewrite exceeds the cost of continuing, not after — the literature is clear that waiting is what makes reconstruction unaffordable.
sources: Brian Foote & Joseph Yoder, 'Big Ball of Mud', PLoP'97 / EuroPLoP'97, Monticello, September 1997; Technical Report #WUCS-97-34; Pattern Languages of Program Design 4, Addison-Wesley, 2000 — definition, the seven patterns (Big Ball of Mud, Throwaway Code, Piecemeal Growth, Keep It Working, Shearing Layers, Sweeping It Under the Rug, Reconstruction), and the argument that mud is a pattern rather than a straw man.
Brian Marick is credited with the term in the University of Illinois Software Architecture Group; the term itself is reported to have arisen during the 1970s as a characterisation of Lisp.

Christopher Alexander, 'The Timeless Way of Building' / 'A Pattern Language' — the fractal-model quote on growth and repair being distributed evenly across all levels of scale, used by Foote and Yoder.
